title: The tax collector's party (Matthew 9:9–13)
hook: Jesus calls Matthew from his booth and eats with his shady friends

segments.voice: Yesterday, disciple: a learner, and fishermen who tried one more time and left full nets on the beach. Your line was put out into the deep. What did you try again? Day fifty-one.

Think of the person in your town nobody wants to sit next to. Maybe they cheated people. Maybe they work for someone everyone resents. Maybe it's just their reputation. Now picture a booth by the road in Capernaum, a fishing town on the lake, where goods passing through get taxed. The man in the booth is named Matthew. He collects money for the rulers who answer to Rome, and people assume, often rightly, that tax collectors took extra for themselves. He's rich, and he's lonely in the way people get when their neighbors look away. Jesus walks past, stops, and looks right at him. Today, the tax collector's party.
screen: `THE ONE NOBODY SITS NEXT TO.` → `A BOOTH BY THE ROAD.` → `JESUS STOPS.`

segments.voice: Two words, in the King James Bible: "Follow me. And he arose, and followed him." No speech. No conditions. Get up. And Matthew does. Then comes the party. Matthew opens his house for a meal, and the text says many publicans and sinners came and sat down with Jesus and his disciples. Publican is the old word for tax collector. Sinners here means people known for breaking the law, the ones good families kept at a distance. Some Pharisees see it. The Pharisees were serious, devout teachers who cared deeply about keeping God's law in everyday life, including who you ate with, because sharing a table meant sharing a life. So they ask the disciples: "Why eateth your Master with publicans and sinners?" It's a real question, and Jesus gives a real answer: "They that be whole need not a physician, but they that are sick." A doctor who avoids sick people isn't much of a doctor. Then he quotes the prophet Hosea, a verse the Pharisees knew well: "I will have mercy, and not sacrifice." Go and learn what that means, he says. And he finishes: "for I am not come to call the righteous, but sinners to repentance." Notice where the calling happens. Not in the temple. At a tax booth, and then at a dinner table. In Mark and Luke the same man is called Levi, and Christian tradition has long said this Matthew is the one whose name is on the first Gospel, though scholars still discuss who wrote it. Either way, the Gospel that bears his name tells his calling in one sentence. He got up.
screen: `FOLLOW ME. AND HE AROSE.` · `A TABLE FULL OF SINNERS.` · `THE WHOLE NEED NO PHYSICIAN.` · `MERCY, AND NOT SACRIFICE.` · then, large: `THEY THAT BE WHOLE NEED NOT A PHYSICIAN.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice. Sit, and let yourself breathe. Now think about your table, whatever that means for you: your lunch spot, your group chat, the people you text back first. Who's always there? Now think of someone who's never there. Someone outside your circle. A coworker who eats alone. A neighbor you've never really met. A relative people roll their eyes at. Picture sharing one ordinary meal with them. What would you talk about? If you pray, you can hold that person before God. The bell holds the time.
The tax collector's party. Matthew gets up from his booth, and Jesus eats at a table full of people others kept away from.
Your line: he came for the sick. This week, share a meal or a coffee with someone outside your circle, even for ten minutes. Day fifty-one.

howItsDone: Many churches keep the feast of Saint Matthew, apostle and evangelist, in September in the West and in November in the Orthodox calendar. Christians often point to this story when welcoming newcomers or sharing meals with people who are left out.

original.note: Greek: a tax or toll collector, from telos, a tax. Matthew's job at the booth.

trapdoor: what you thought: Jesus goes to a party.
what it means: Jesus calls a man everyone avoided, then eats at his table with the people good families kept away from.
what a scholar hears: sharing a table in that world meant sharing a life, so the meal itself made the point, and the answer he gave came from Hosea 6:6.

notes: The index hook says 'dodgy friends' (British informal); the script's hook line says 'shady friends' for American spelling and usage. The index is left as it is.

Tax booth location: Matthew 9:1 places Jesus in 'his own city' (Capernaum per Matthew 4:13); the booth was likely a toll office on goods. Tax collectors in Galilee served Herod Antipas, who ruled under Rome; the script says 'rulers who answer to Rome'.
Pharisees are described respectfully and the question is presented as sincere, to avoid a caricature of Jewish teachers. Confirm.
Authorship of Matthew's Gospel: tradition (Papias, Irenaeus) credits the apostle; many modern scholars doubt it. Stated neutrally.
Feast of Saint Matthew: September 21 (Western), November 16 (Orthodox). Confirm.
Original: τελώνης (Matthew 9:10–11 uses the plural τελῶναι).
